design_comparison.belongs_to_appendix: Part I plates depict the novel's worlds (courts, rooms, streets, bodies in motion) in gold; these depict the novel's paperwork about those worlds (floor-plans, catalogues, transcripts, letters, labels, colophons) in violet. The threshold plate is a plan, not a place; the broadsheet is a catalogue, not a cinema; the confession is a badge, not a face. Put a Part I title on any of these and the violet apparatus reads as filing furniture for a story happening elsewhere -- which is exactly what endnotes are.
design_comparison.chosen: C, hardened: every plate is an engraved office object drawn from the notes' own nouns (cardioid, cartridge spine, wheel, cassette, pail, press badge, portrait row, badge variant, rail ties, bench, apothecary bottle, endmark), composed as plate furniture with mono caption bands, violet keylines, and one textual wink per plate (dent, IJ-V sigil, sic, ®) that only a reader of the notes gets.
considered: A. Pure index furniture: 12 variations of ruled cards, tabs, numerals. Rejected -- honest to the appendix but visually monotonous; violates the ambition bar and repeats the Part I ledger frame with nothing new to look at.

B. Illustrative scenes from note content (Hal soaking his ankle, the six boys on the rails, the locker room). Rejected -- competes with Part I's world-depicting plates, risks kitsch literalism (Cage III eyeballs, feral infants), and misreads the notes as story rather than apparatus.

C. Apparatus-as-artifact: each plate is the physical document-object the note-group resembles (floor-plan, broadsheet, primer seal, cassette, triptych file, press badge, yearbook page, confession file, letterhead+rail diagram, locker bench, apothecary shelf, colophon endmark). Chosen.
